name: Hime gyaru

card.summary: A Japanese gyaru style built around big curled and teased hair, rococo-inspired pink dresses and dramatic eye makeup, used to create a doll-like princess look.
card.note: Costly brands and daily styling; hair is often bleached and curled.

quick.overview:
Hime gyaru, meaning princess gyaru, is one of the most flamboyant substyles of Japanese gyaru fashion. The look combines voluminous curled hair, exaggerated eye makeup and pastel pink lace-and-bow clothing to create a rococo, doll-like princess appearance.

It grew in the early 2000s, with a more casual spin-off called himekaji peaking between 2010 and 2013. It is a fashion style rather than a studied intervention, so documentation comes from encyclopedias and gyaru magazines rather than studies.
quick.how: People put the look together with bleached or light hair crimped into a bouffant on top, often with curled extensions or wigs, bold eye makeup, and pink or pastel dresses with lace, roses, pearls and crowns. Many fans treat it as a lifestyle and decorate homes to match. Brands associated with it include Jesus Diamante, La Parfait and Princess Melody, with Rosy Future as a cheaper option.
quick.risks: Costs are high for the expensive brands, and bleaching and heated styling can stress hair. The style is time-intensive. No health studies address it specifically.

lead: Hime gyaru (hime kei, 'princess gyaru') is a substyle of Japanese gyaru fashion described as one of its most flamboyant and expensive.[1] It draws on Rococo-era aesthetics and aims at a princess-like, feminine, doll-like look through voluminous curled hair, dramatic eyes and pastel dresses.[1]

Wikipedia says hime gyaru blossomed in the early 2000s and later declined, while a more casual offshoot, himekaji or 'princess casual', emerged in the late 2000s and peaked between 2010 and 2013.[1][2]
The look is built on hair, makeup and clothing choices that practitioners assemble to change their appearance, and it is part of the wider gyaru history of Shibuya, magazines and 109 stores.[2]

chain: Bleached, bouffant curled hair and wigs add volume
Exaggerated eye makeup and pastel rococo clothing
angle.text: The style changes appearance directly through hair volume, makeup and clothing. Followers use it to create an ornate feminine look.

paras: Wikipedia describes the clothing as pink or pastel dresses and skirts with lace and bows, with rose patterns, rosettes, pearls and crown motifs. Hair is bleached and crimped into a bouffant, with curled wigs or extensions for volume, and eye makeup is more exaggerated than in typical gyaru.[1]

Brands such as Jesus Diamante, La Parfait and Princess Melody are named as expensive labels, and Rosy Future as a cheaper one.[1] Some fans treat the style as a lifestyle, extending it to home decoration.[1]

Gyaru culture developed through the 1970s to 2000s, centred on Shibuya's department stores and magazines such as egg, Popteen and Koakuma Ageha.[2] Hime gyaru appeared in the early 2000s, and magazines carried hime titles such as Hime!, Hime Style and Hime nail.[1][2]

Himekaji, a casual version linked with Liz Lisa, Axes Femme and similar brands, uses a pink and white palette without requiring tanning, peaked from 2010 to 2013 and has seen an online resurgence.[2] Both Wikipedia pages carry notices that parts may be unreliable.

timeline.event: Hime gyaru emerges as a rococo-inspired gyaru substyle.[1]
